title: Mysterious Core Forces Shift Earth’s Day Length, Scientists Reveal New Findings
body:
Scientists have long treated the 24‑hour day as a fixed unit, but new research shows that the planet’s rotation is anything but constant. A suite of subtle forces—ranging from shifting ocean currents to the planet’s own internal dynamics—periodically speed up or slow down Earth’s spin, causing the length of a solar day to vary by milliseconds over years and centuries. While the changes are too small to affect daily life, they have profound implications for precise time‑keeping, satellite navigation and our understanding of Earth’s interior.

The most recent study, conducted by an international team of geophysicists, combined satellite laser ranging, very‑long‑baseline interferometry and historical astronomical observations to produce the most comprehensive model to date of Earth’s rotational variability. Their analysis confirms that the planet’s day can be up to 1.7 milliseconds longer or shorter than the nominal 86,400 seconds, depending on the interplay of several mechanisms. The researchers identified three primary contributors: tidal friction caused by the Moon’s gravitational pull, mass redistribution within Earth’s fluid envelopes (oceans, atmosphere, and liquid outer core), and the less‑understood motions of the solid mantle and inner core.

Tidal friction has been recognized for centuries as a driver of gradual deceleration; the Moon’s pull raises ocean bulges that lag behind the Earth’s rotation, converting kinetic energy into heat and lengthening the day by about 2.3 milliseconds per century. However, the new findings highlight that this long‑term trend is punctuated by shorter‑term fluctuations. Seasonal shifts in atmospheric pressure and wind patterns can transfer angular momentum between the atmosphere and the solid Earth, temporarily accelerating rotation by a few microseconds. Likewise, large‑scale oceanic phenomena such as El Niño and the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation can redistribute water mass, subtly altering the planet’s moment of inertia and thus its spin rate.

Perhaps the most intriguing discovery concerns the deep interior. Seismic tomography and geomagnetic data suggest that the liquid outer core and the solid inner core are not perfectly synchronized with the mantle. Differential rotation between these layers can induce minute changes in Earth’s angular momentum. The study reports evidence of a quasi‑decadal oscillation, likely tied to core‑mantle coupling, that adds or subtracts up to 0.2 milliseconds from the length of the day. This internal “heartbeat” of the planet is still being unraveled, but it underscores how Earth’s deep structure participates in a dynamic system that extends far beyond surface processes.

These variations matter most to fields that rely on ultra‑precise timing. Global navigation satellite systems (GNSS), such as GPS, GLONASS and Galileo, must account for minute changes in Earth’s rotation to maintain positional accuracy within centimeters. Similarly, astronomical observatories and deep‑space missions use Earth’s rotation as a reference frame; uncorrected drifts could accumulate into significant errors over long missions. The International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service (IERS) already publishes daily updates on Earth Orientation Parameters, but the new model promises to improve forecast reliability, allowing engineers and scientists to anticipate rotational shifts weeks or months in advance.

Looking ahead, the researchers advocate for a more integrated monitoring network that fuses satellite gravimetry, oceanic buoy data, and high‑resolution seismic observations. By tracking how mass moves within the oceans, atmosphere and mantle in near real‑time, scientists could refine predictions of day‑length fluctuations and better understand the feedback loops between Earth’s interior and its surface environment. As climate change reshapes ocean circulation and atmospheric dynamics, these feedbacks may become more pronounced, potentially altering the already delicate balance of forces that govern our planet’s spin. Continued investment in interdisciplinary Earth‑system observation will be essential not only for maintaining the precision of our clocks and navigation systems but also for deepening our grasp of the hidden processes that keep Earth turning.
